title: (Scenario) How would you introduce a breaking event-schema change used by 15 consumers — why must you avoid requiring fifteen teams to deploy at the same moment (use a compatibility strategy: additive evolution, a new event version, dual publication during a controlled period, or consumer changes before producer changes), and why is the technical schema only part of the problem (once fifteen teams depend on an event, changing it becomes an organizational migration)?
shortTitle: How would you introduce a breaking event-schema change used by 15 consumers?

s1_definition.profdef: A breaking event-schema change is one where new events can no longer be understood by consumers written against the old schema — a removed or renamed field, a changed type, or a changed meaning. When fifteen independent consumers depend on the event, you cannot flip the schema in one deployment because that would require all fifteen teams to deploy at exactly the same instant, which is operationally impossible and catastrophic if even one is late. The solution is a compatibility strategy that decouples the producer's change from the consumers' changes in time: evolve additively so old consumers keep working; or publish a new versioned event alongside the old one (dual publication) for a controlled period; or require consumers to be upgraded to tolerate the new form before the producer switches. The technical schema is only half the problem, because once fifteen teams depend on an event, changing it is fundamentally an organizational migration requiring coordination, communication, deprecation timelines, and ownership, not just a code edit.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India sends a standard "transaction completed" slip to fifteen different departments — fraud, statements, rewards, tax, audit, and so on — and each department has built its own process around reading that exact slip. Now the bank wants to change the slip's format in a way that breaks the old readers. If the bank just prints the new slip tomorrow, every department that has not updated its process at the same minute suddenly cannot read it, and fraud detection or audit goes blind. So instead the bank either adds new fields without removing old ones so everyone keeps reading what they rely on, or it prints both the old slip and a new slip for a few months while each department migrates on its own schedule, or it asks every department to first learn to read the new slip before the bank stops printing the old one. And critically, the bank has to actually talk to fifteen department heads, agree a timeline, and track who has migrated — the format is the easy part.
s1_definition.oneliner: Never force fifteen teams to deploy at one instant — evolve additively or dual-publish a versioned event through a controlled deprecation, and treat the change as an organizational migration, not a schema edit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A breaking event-schema change is one where new events can no longer be understood by consumers written against the old schema — a removed or renamed field, a changed type, or a changed meaning. The technical schema is only half the problem, because once fifteen teams depend on an event, changing it is fundamentally an organizational migration requiring coordination, communication, deprecation timelines, and ownership, not just a code edit.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India sends a standard "transaction completed" slip to fifteen different departments — fraud, statements, rewards, tax, audit, and so on — and each department has built its own process around reading that exact slip. Now the bank wants to change the slip's format in a way that breaks the old readers. If the bank just prints the new slip tomorrow, every department that has not updated its process at the same minute suddenly cannot read it, and fraud detection or audit goes blind. So instead the bank either adds new fields without removing old ones so everyone keeps reading what they rely on, or it prints both the old slip and a new slip for a few months while each department migrates on its own schedule, or it asks every department to first learn to read the new slip before the bank stops printing the old one. **One line to remember:** Never force fifteen teams to deploy at one instant — evolve additively or dual-publish a versioned event through a controlled deprecation, and treat the change as an organizational migration, not a schema edit.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a payments service publishes a `TransferCompleted` event consumed by fifteen downstream services — fraud detection, statements, rewards, tax reporting, audit, and others. The team must change the amount field from a floating representation to integer paise, which is a breaking change.

Problem 1 — flipping the field in one deploy would break every consumer not updated at the same instant. With fifteen teams on fifteen schedules, a simultaneous deploy is impossible, and the first consumer to miss the window goes blind — including fraud and audit, which is unacceptable for a bank.

Problem 2 — the change is not purely additive because the amount field's type is changing, so simply adding a field is not enough unless old consumers can keep reading the old field.

The fix dual-publishes a v1 event with the old amount field and a v2 event with the integer-paise field during a controlled deprecation window, tracks which consumers have migrated, and retires v1 only when the registry shows zero v1 consumers. The mini-project builds an `EventBus`, a `Producer` that dual-publishes v1 and v2, a set of `Consumer`s on different versions, and a `MigrationTracker` that records each consumer's version and decides when v1 can be safely retired. The demo shows old consumers working on v1, new ones on v2, and v1 being retired only after the tracker confirms full migration.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a payments service emits transfer-completed events consumed by fraud and statements, with the amount field changing from decimal to integer paise.

Step 1 — Window opens, both consumers on v1. Fraud and statements subscribe to the v1 topic. The migration tracker records both as v1. The producer is configured to dual-publish.

Step 2 — First transfer published. For TRF-1, the producer emits both a v1 event with the decimal amount and a v2 event with the paise amount. Fraud and statements each receive the v1 event and process it exactly as before. The breaking change has been introduced without breaking anyone.

Step 3 — Fraud migrates to v2. The fraud team deploys on its own schedule, subscribes to the v2 topic, and the tracker records fraud as v2. When the producer asks whether v1 can be retired, the tracker answers no, because statements is still on v1, and logs exactly which consumer is holding v1 open.

Step 4 — Statements migrates to v2. Later, the statements team migrates, and the tracker records statements as v2. For TRF-2, both still receive events during the overlap, but now every consumer can read v2.

Step 5 — v1 retired safely. With every consumer confirmed on v2, the tracker says v1 can be retired, so the producer stops publishing v1. TRF-3 is published as v2 only. The breaking change is fully rolled out, and at no point did two teams have to deploy at the same instant.

```

2026-10-24 18:55:12 [INFO] statements now on v1
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Compatibility Strategy ═══

  ┌─ Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Versioned Event + Dual Publication (parallel-change)       │
  │ Additive Evolution (add optional fields, never remove)     │
  │ Consumer Inventory + Deprecation Window (organizational)   │
  │ Schema Registry compatibility check at publish time        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Producer publishes; Tracker tracks; Consumers consume   │
  │ O: new version = new topic + mapping, old path unchanged   │
  │ D: consumers depend on an event contract, not the producer │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────┐ publishes ┌──────────────┐ delivers ┌──────────────┐
  │ TransferProducer │──────────▶│ EventBus     │─────────▶│ Consumers    │
  │ + completeTransfer│          │ + publish()  │          │ onV1()/onV2()│
  │ + stopPublishingV1│          └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │ consults
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ MigrationTracker │  canRetireV1()
  └──────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: v1 lifecycle ──
  [v1 ONLY] ──introduce v2──→ [DUAL (v1+v2)] ──all consumers migrated──→ [v2 ONLY]
                                     │ any consumer still v1
                                     └── stay DUAL (window stays open)

  ── Call Chain (main) ──
  1. producer.completeTransfer(TRF-1)  → publish v1 + v2
  2. fraud migrates → tracker.register("fraud","v2")
  3. tracker.canRetireV1() → false (statements on v1)
  4. statements migrates → tracker.register("statements","v2")
  5. tracker.canRetireV1() → true → producer.stopPublishingV1()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason I would never flip the event schema in a single deployment is coupling in time. An event consumed by fifteen teams has fifteen independent deployment schedules, fifteen on-call rotations, and fifteen backlogs, so requiring all of them to deploy at the exact same instant as the producer is a distributed lockstep that is guaranteed to fail — one team is mid-incident, one is frozen for a release, one is on holiday — and the moment the producer switches, every consumer that has not caught up breaks, possibly including fraud detection or audit, which for a bank is unacceptable. So the whole strategy is about buying time by letting the producer's change and the consumers' changes happen on independent schedules.

My first choice is always additive evolution. If I only add new optional fields and never remove, rename, or repurpose existing ones, old consumers simply ignore the new fields and keep working while new consumers read them, and no coordinated deploy is needed at all. Most changes that look breaking can be made additive if I am willing to leave the old field in place during the transition. When the change genuinely cannot be additive — for example, a field's type or meaning must change — I publish a new event version alongside the old one and dual-publish both for a controlled deprecation window. Old consumers keep reading v1, each team migrates to v2 on its own schedule, and only after every consumer has moved and I have verified v1 has zero remaining readers do I stop publishing v1. A schema registry with backward-compatibility enforcement makes this safe by rejecting incompatible changes at publish time.

But the part I would emphasise most in an interview is that the technical schema is only half the problem. The moment fifteen teams depend on my event, that event is a contract, and changing a contract with fifteen counterparties is an organizational migration, not a code edit. I have to discover who actually consumes the event — there are almost always undocumented consumers — publish a clear deprecation timeline, communicate it, provide the new schema and migration guidance, track every consumer's migration status, and retire the old version only when that tracking confirms zero usage. In my banking work the failure mode was never "the schema was wrong"; it was "we broke a consumer we did not know existed" or "a team ran out of runway before the window closed."

So the design I would present has equal technical and organizational halves: the compatibility technique — additive fields or a versioned, dual-published event behind a schema registry — buys the time, and the consumer inventory, the deprecation window, the status dashboard, and the communication plan are what actually get fifteen teams across the line. The principle I carry is that you measure the success of an event-schema change not by how clean the new schema is, but by the fact that no team was ever forced to deploy on someone else's clock, and no consumer went blind because of a change it did not see coming.
